newsitem.title: CHINA: China TV price war hurts foreign makers.
newsitem.headline: China TV price war hurts foreign makers.

text.p: A colour television price war in China is spurring sales, cutting the share of foreign brands and rationalising an industry which has capacity of nearly three times demand, company officials and newspapers said on Monday.
The war was launched in March by market leader, Sichuan Chang Hong Electric Co with price cuts of eight to 18 percent. Other top domestic producers followed suit.

The result was a rise in market share of the major Chinese producers and a drop in the share held by foreign brands and small and medium-size Chinese makers, the Shanghai Securities News reported on Monday.

Because of the price cut, Chang Hong's market share rose to 26 percent in October from 16 percent in March, with sales rising by 1.3 million sets, overtaking Matsushita Electric Industry as the top seller, it said.
Chang Hong expects total 1996 sales of 4.5 million sets, up from 2.6 million in 1995 out of total national output of 19.58 million sets, up 15.9 percent over the 1994 level.

"Before, Chinese consumers used to prefer foreign brands over domestic ones but now think they are about the same," said an official of Matsushita's Shanghai office. "This applies to refrigerators and motorcycles as well as colour televisions."
"The price war has affected foreign brands because domestic technology has started to mature," he said.

A survey published in the China Business Times newspaper said that, because of the price war, domestic brands accounted for 68 percent of the domestic colour television market in August, up from 55 percent in March.

In small and medium-size cities, the market share of domestic brands was more than 70 percent, but foreign brands still ruled in major cities, with 84 percent in Guangzhou and 61 percent in Shanghai, it said.
It said that, because of the price cuts, total sales of colour televisions in China this year would rise 15 percent from the 1995 level to around 17.3 million sets.
The Shanghai Securities News said the fierce market competition this year had resulted in a restructuring of historical proportions in China's television industry.
China has nearly 100 manufacturers whose total capacity is nearly three times the annual demand. Foreign joint ventures have an annual output capacity of nearly eight million sets, it said.
The losers in this rationalisation are dozens of small manufacturers whose market share is falling and who lack the scale of production to compete with the big players.
An official of Chang Hong said that it was discussing a friendly takeover of several small and medium-size makers but declined to give details of the negotiations.
An official of Shenzhen Konka Electronic (Group) Co Ltd, the second biggest domestic producer, said it would in 1997 take over a small maker in east China, similar to an acquisition it made in 1993.
In February that year it paid 18 million yuan ($2.17 million) for 60 percent of a television factory in Mudanjiang in the northeast province of Heilongjiang that was close to bankruptcy.
